entries.text_de:
Cambridge Corpus Christi College 265, einst dem Domkloster Worcester gehörig, um 10253, enthält zumeist kanonistische und theologische Auszüge, grossentheils Lateinisch, z. Th. Fränkischer Herkunft.

p. 217 um 1040 IV Eg Versio, u. S. 207; p. 222 IV Eg, u. S. 206.

Auf f. 211a4: Incipit excommunicatio contra contemptores legis Domini et inimicos sancte Dei ęcclesię. Pro lectione sancti evangelii ascendat diaconus pulpitum et legat excommunicationem, ita dicens: Audite, fratres karissimi, quod nunc provocati agimus. Omnipotens Dominus ad benedicendum nos constituit, non ad maledicendum. Sed quia non est societas Christi cum Belial. — Aus C copirte Hk und Vs.
entries.text_en:
Cambridge Corpus Christi College 265, once belonging to the cathedral priory of Worcester, c. 10253; contains mostly canonistic and theological extracts, largely in Latin, partly of Frankish origin.

p. 217, c. 1040, IV Eg Versio, below, p. 207; p. 222 IV Eg, below, p. 206.

On f. 211a4: Incipit excommunicatio contra contemptores legis Domini et inimicos sancte Dei ęcclesię. Pro lectione sancti evangelii ascendat diaconus pulpitum et legat excommunicationem, ita dicens: Audite, fratres karissimi, quod nunc provocati agimus. Omnipotens Dominus ad benedicendum nos constituit, non ad maledicendum. Sed quia non est societas Christi cum Belial. — Hk and Vs copied from C.

transcription.doubts: Latin left untranslated (as Liebermann prints it). 'Selborn' as printed (= Selborne). The page reference switches from 'p.' to 'f. 211a' as printed.

wormald.wormald_date: s. xi^med (Table 4.1, p. 164; Ker's date, p. 211 n. 193); additions from p. 269 s. xi², s. xi/xii and early twelfth century (p. 211 n. 193; p. 219 n. 221); a book from after Wulfstan's time (p. 218); later of the pair with CCCC 190 (p. 211)
wormald.wormald_origin: Worcester (Table 4.1, p. 164): 'undoubtedly a Worcester MS' — a monastic profession to Bishop Wulfstan II added on the front flyleaf; at Worcester in the sixteenth century, when Joscelyn annotated it (p. 219 and n. 219). Later sections c)–d) may reflect Bishop Ealdred and/or Wulfstan II (p. 219).
wormald.laws: IV Eg, in Latin and Old English, in section b) (MS pp. 209–36, quires 14–15), preceded by formulae for excommunication (MS pp. 211–13) and absolution, and followed by the Maundy Thursday blessing of oils (Wormald pp. 211–12, 219). The excommunication formulae are like those Liebermann printed as Excom, but he did not print these (p. 211 n. 196).
wormald.other_contents: Section a) (pp. 1–208): the Wulfstan 'Canon Collection' — Admonitio spiritalis doctrinae, Admonitio episcopalis vitae, letters of Alcuin, Irish canons on bishops, Ghaerbald's capitulary fronting the 'Excerptiones de libris canonicis', penitential texts incl. Ecgberht's penitential, Abbo's Maundy Thursday sermon (pp. 142–8), OE 'Directions for a Confessor' (p. 72, the only vernacular text in a)), Aachen 816 on clerical ranks, Hrabanus etc. (Table 4.4, pp. 214–15). Section b): an added condemnation (p. 209) of men who burned and plundered St Mary's land 'æt Christes hala … æt ontelawe'; unfinished sketch-map of Noah's descendants and the apostles' missions (p. 210). Section c): Ælfric's letter to the monks of Eynsham (his version of the Regularis Concordia) with Amalarius extracts. Section d): parts of the Romano-German pontifical and more Amalarius (pp. 269–442 liturgica). 265 × 165 mm, 26 lines (pp. 211–19).
wormald.overview: Corpus 265 is a mid-eleventh-century Worcester compendium of canon law, penitential and liturgical texts for a working bishop, whose first part is among the most systematic surviving forms of the canon collection associated with Archbishop Wulfstan. Its separate second section contains IV Edgar, uniquely in both Latin and Old English, set between formulae for excommunicating and absolving enemies of the Church and the Maundy Thursday rite for reconciling penitents — a placing Wormald explains by the code's insistence on tithe. The Latin version, he suggests, was made so that a royal code could take its place in a learned Latin collection of church law, and a related twelfth-century collection (Barlow 37) hints that IV Edgar may have belonged to the collection from an early stage.
wormald.pages: 211–19 (Table 4.4, pp. 214–15); 164 (Table 4.1); 184 (IV Eg’s ‘other manuscript’, kin to Nero E.i); 220–1; 223
wormald.key_quote: a secular code was being enrolled in the learned law of the Church (p. 219)
wormald.doubts: GUIDE: Liebermann's date 'c. 1025; p. 217 c. 1040' — Wormald (following Ker) dates the book s. xi^med and stresses it is after Wulfstan's time; section b) (IV Eg) is mainly in one hand, not that of all of a), with a second scribe on MS pp. 211, 215 (p. 212 n. 201). GUIDE: the guide lists 'Excom' for C, but Wormald (p. 211 n. 196) says Liebermann did not print the CCCC 265 excommunication formulae (he printed Excom III from CCCC 190) — check whether Liebermann only mentioned them in his description. Other sigla: 'X' for the Homily editors, 'Z' for Aronstam; Ker no. 53. Hk and Vs copies (guide) not mentioned by Wormald here. Ker’s ‘s xi^med’ and additions ‘s xi², s xi/xii’ checked in image (p. 211 n. 193). Page references in other_contents are to MS pages.
verify_notes: laws: distinguished MS pages from Wormald’s pages; excommunication/absolution precede and oils follow IV Eg (pp. 211–12).
overview: ‘the most systematic’ softened to ‘among the most systematic’ (p. 217 puts CCCC 265 and Nero A.i together).
pages: added 184 (Wormald calls it the code’s other manuscript, ‘close kin and perhaps descendant’ of Nero E.i).

laws_note.text: Liebermann did not print the excommunication formulae in this manuscript (his Excom texts come from other manuscripts).

notes.text: Once belonging to Worcester cathedral priory, mainly canon-law and theological extracts, largely Latin; contains IV Edgar in Latin version and in English, and an excommunication formula against despisers of God's law. Hk and Vs were copied from C.

Corpus 265 is a mid-eleventh-century Worcester compendium of canon law, penitential and liturgical texts for a working bishop, whose first part is among the most systematic surviving forms of the canon collection associated with Archbishop Wulfstan. Its separate second section contains IV Edgar, uniquely in both Latin and Old English, set between formulae for excommunicating and absolving enemies of the Church and the Maundy Thursday rite for reconciling penitents — a placing Wormald explains by the code's insistence on tithe. The Latin version, he suggests, was made so that a royal code could take its place in a learned Latin collection of church law, and a related twelfth-century collection (Barlow 37) hints that IV Edgar may have belonged to the collection from an early stage.
